statement: If $f$ is a [univalent function](c:univalent-function) on the [unit disc](c:unit-disc) with $f(0) = 0$, then $f$ maps every disc $|z| < r$ with $r \le \tanh(\pi/4)$ onto a [starlike](c:starlike) domain.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [univalent](c:univalent-function) on the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$.
The function $f$ satisfies $f(0) = 0$.
The radius satisfies $0 < r \le \tanh(\pi/4)$.

conclusion: The domain $f(\{|z| < r\})$ is [starlike](c:starlike) with respect to $0$.

proofs.name: Löwner chain and Grunsky's inequality
proofs.slogan: Bound $\log(zf'(z)/f(z))$ along a Löwner chain, then compare the bound with $\pi/2$ to get starlikeness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, after the normalization $f'(0) = 1$ and the reduction to slit maps. The proof is an outline of Grunsky's argument; the Löwner theory (density of slit maps, Löwner's equation) rests on the cited books.

roles.why: Univalence gives $f'(0) \ne 0$, the Löwner chain, and simple image curves in the last step.
The condition $f(0) = 0$ gives the normalization $f(z) = z + \cdots$ and the base point $0$ of starlikeness.
The bound on $r$ keeps the logarithmic bound below $\pi/2$.

steps.slogan: Normalize $f$ and reduce to slit maps.
steps.detail: Univalence gives $f'(0) \ne 0$, and dividing $f$ by $f'(0)$ does not change the shape of any image. So assume $f(z) = z + \cdots$. Slit maps are dense in this class (Löwner), and a locally uniform limit of maps with $\mathrm{Re}\,zf'/f \ge 0$ on $|z| < r$ keeps that property, so slit maps suffice.

steps.slogan: Embed the slit map in a Löwner chain of transition maps.
steps.detail: For a slit map there are maps $\psi(z,t)$ of the disc into itself with $\psi(z,0) = z$ and $\partial_t \psi = -\psi\,(1 + \kappa\psi)/(1 - \kappa\psi)$, where $|\kappa(t)| = 1$ (the [Löwner equation](c:lowner-equation)). They satisfy $f(z) = \lim_{t \to \infty} e^t \psi(z,t)$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the flow to get an equation for $q = z\psi_z/\psi$.
steps.detail: Put $w = \kappa\psi$. Applying $z\,\partial_z$ to the Löwner equation for $\log\psi$ gives $\partial_t \log q = -2w/(1-w)^2$ with $q(z,0) = 1$. As $t \to \infty$, $q(z,t)$ tends to $zf'(z)/f(z)$, because $\psi(z,t) \to 0$ and $e^{-t}f_t$ is a normalized univalent function.

steps.slogan: Bound $|\log q|$ by the decrease of $|\psi|$ along the flow.
steps.detail: Let $\rho = |\psi|$. The Löwner equation gives $\rho' = -\rho(1-\rho^2)/|1-w|^2$, while $|\partial_t \log q| = 2\rho/|1-w|^2 = -2\rho'/(1-\rho^2)$. Integrating while $\rho$ falls from $|z|$ gives $|\log q| \le \int_0^{|z|} 2\,d\rho/(1-\rho^2) = \log\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}$.

steps.slogan: Compare the bound with $\pi/2$ to get $\mathrm{Re}\,zf'/f > 0$.
steps.detail: Letting $t \to \infty$ gives Grunsky's inequality $|\log(zf'(z)/f(z))| \le \log\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|}$. The right side equals $\pi/2$ exactly when $|z| = \tanh(\pi/4)$, so it is below $\pi/2$ for $|z| < r$. Hence $|\arg(zf'/f)| < \pi/2$, that is $\mathrm{Re}\,zf'/f > 0$ on $|z| < r$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that every disc $|z| < r$ maps onto a [starlike](c:starlike) domain.
steps.detail: On a circle $|z| = \rho < r$, the curve $\theta \mapsto f(\rho e^{i\theta})$ is simple, and $\frac{d}{d\theta}\arg f = \mathrm{Re}\,zf'/f > 0$. So it turns monotonically around $0$, and the image of $|z| < r$ is starlike with respect to $0$. The normalization of step 1 transfers the result to every $f$ with $f(0) = 0$.

concepts.c:univalent-function: Univalent maps are the class embedded in Löwner chains.
concepts.c:unit-disc: The Löwner flow moves points of the unit disc towards $0$.
concepts.c:starlike: Starlikeness is the property that the logarithmic bound establishes.
concepts.c:lowner-equation: The Löwner equation drives the flow whose logarithmic derivative is estimated.

source.ref: H. Grunsky, Zwei Bemerkungen zur konformen Abbildung, Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung 43 (1934), 140-142; Loewner theory as in C. Pommerenke, Univalent Functions, Vandenhoeck and Ruprecht, Goettingen, 1975, and P. L. Duren, Univalent Functions, Springer, 1983
source.note: Steps 1 and 2 use Löwner's density theorem and differential equation from the cited books; steps 3 and 4 derive Grunsky's inequality |log(zf'/f)| <= log((1+|z|)/(1-|z|)) from that equation.

statement: Let $G$ be a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) and $\Theta$ an [invariant eigendistribution](c:invariant-eigendistribution) on $G$. Then $\Theta$ is given by a locally integrable function $F$ on $G$ that is analytic on the regular set $G'$: $\Theta(\varphi) = \int_G F\varphi\,dx$ for every test function $\varphi$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group).
The distribution $\Theta$ on $G$ is invariant under conjugation by $G$.
The distribution $\Theta$ is an eigendistribution of the center $\mathfrak{Z}$ of the universal enveloping algebra: $z\Theta = \chi(z)\Theta$ for every $z \in \mathfrak{Z}$.

conclusion: A locally integrable function $F$, analytic on the regular set $G'$, represents $\Theta$.

proofs.name: Radial parts and descent
proofs.slogan: Show analyticity on the regular set, descend to centralizers, bound $|D|^{1/2}F$, and identify the distribution with the function.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a real connected semisimple group, as an outline of Harish-Chandra's proof. A [character](c:character-of-a-representation) of an irreducible unitary representation is an invariant eigendistribution, so it is a function; the p-adic case is a separate theorem.

roles.why: Semisimplicity gives Cartan subgroups, the Weyl denominator $D$ and the centralizers used in the descent.
Invariance lets $\Theta$ be studied through its restrictions to Cartan subgroups.
The eigenvalue equations give the radial equations that force analyticity and the bound on $|D|^{1/2}F$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Theta$ is an analytic function on the regular set.
steps.detail: On the open dense set $G'$, the conjugation-invariant $\Theta$ is determined by its restriction to each Cartan subgroup $H$. After multiplying by the Weyl denominator, the eigenvalue equations become a constant-coefficient system on $H$ whose only common characteristic point is $0$. So the restriction is an analytic function $F$ on $G'$.

steps.slogan: Descend to the Lie algebra of a centralizer near a singular point.
steps.detail: Near an element with semisimple part $s$, the exponential map identifies a neighborhood with a neighborhood in the centralizer of $s$ and then in its Lie algebra. There $\Theta$ becomes an invariant eigendistribution on a smaller reductive group or Lie algebra. This allows induction on $\dim G$, with the Lie algebra case treated by the Fourier transform.

steps.slogan: Bound $|D|^{1/2}F$ locally with the radial equations and the induction.
steps.detail: Harish-Chandra's estimates for the solutions of the radial equations, together with the induction of step 2, show that $|D|^{1/2}F$ is locally bounded near every point of $G$. The Weyl integration formula makes $|D|^{-1/2}$ locally integrable, so $F$ is locally integrable on $G$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $\Theta$ equals $F$ across the singular set.
steps.detail: The difference $\Theta - F$ is an invariant eigendistribution that vanishes on $G'$, so it is supported on the singular set $G \setminus G'$. The descent of step 2 and induction on the dimension of the support show that such a distribution is zero. So $\Theta = F$ as distributions.

concepts.c:semisimple-lie-group: Semisimplicity supplies Cartan subgroups and the Weyl denominator.
concepts.c:invariant-eigendistribution: These are the distributions that the proof shows to be functions.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: Characters of irreducible unitary representations are the main examples.

source.ref: Harish-Chandra, Invariant eigendistributions on a semisimple Lie group, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 119 (1965), 457-508
source.note: The steps outline the radial-part, descent and estimate arguments of this paper and of Harish-Chandra's Lie algebra paper, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES 27 (1965), 5-54.

statement: Let $K \subset \mathbb{C}$ be [compact](c:compact-space) with [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) zero. Then every continuous function $f\colon K \to \mathbb{C}$ admits [uniform rational approximation](c:rational-approximation): for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a rational function $R$ with poles off $K$ and $|f - R| < \varepsilon$ on $K$.

hypotheses.text: The set $K \subset \mathbb{C}$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
The set $K$ has area zero: $\lambda(K) = 0$ for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $\lambda$ on $\mathbb{C}$.
The function $f\colon K \to \mathbb{C}$ is continuous.

conclusion: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a [rational function](c:rational-function) $R$ with poles outside $K$ and $\sup_K |f - R| < \varepsilon$.

proofs.name: Cauchy transform of an annihilating measure
proofs.slogan: Show by duality that a measure annihilating all rational functions is zero, using its Cauchy transform and the area-zero hypothesis.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for nonempty $K$; for $K = \emptyset$ there is nothing to prove. Sets of positive area need the deeper theorem of Mergelyan.

roles.why: [Compactness](c:compact-space) makes $C(K)$ a Banach space whose dual consists of measures on $K$.
Area zero lets the Cauchy transform vanish almost everywhere, since it vanishes off $K$.
The function $f$ is an element of $C(K)$ that the duality argument approximates.

steps.slogan: Reduce density to a measure that annihilates every rational function.
steps.detail: Let $R(K)$ be the uniform closure in $C(K)$ of the rational functions with poles off $K$. If $R(K) \ne C(K)$, the Hahn-Banach theorem gives a nonzero bounded functional vanishing on $R(K)$. By the Riesz representation theorem it is a complex measure $\mu \ne 0$ on $K$ with $\int R\,d\mu = 0$ for every such $R$.

steps.slogan: Define the Cauchy transform $\hat\mu(z) = \int d\mu(w)/(w - z)$ and show that it is locally integrable.
steps.detail: Let $K \subset \{|w| \le M\}$. For every $w \in K$, $\int_{|z| \le M} dA(z)/|w - z| \le 4\pi M$. By Fubini, $\int_{|z| \le M} |\hat\mu|\,dA \le 4\pi M\,\|\mu\|$, so $\hat\mu$ is defined almost everywhere and is locally integrable.

steps.slogan: Show that the Cauchy transform vanishes almost everywhere.
steps.detail: For $z \notin K$, the function $w \mapsto 1/(w - z)$ is rational with its pole off $K$, so $\hat\mu(z) = 0$ by the choice of $\mu$. The set $K$ has area zero, so $\hat\mu = 0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb{C}$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\partial\hat\mu/\partial\bar z$ in the sense of distributions.
steps.detail: For a test function $\varphi$ with compact support, the Cauchy-Pompeiu formula gives $\int \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\bar z}(z)\,\frac{dA(z)}{w - z} = \pi\varphi(w)$. Fubini then gives $\int \hat\mu\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\bar z}\,dA = \pi\int \varphi\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\mu = 0$, which contradicts the choice of $\mu$.
steps.detail: Since $\hat\mu = 0$ almost everywhere, step 4 gives $\int \varphi\,d\mu = 0$ for every test function $\varphi$. Restrictions of test functions are dense in $C(K)$ by the Stone-Weierstrass theorem, so $\mu = 0$. This contradicts step 1, so $R(K) = C(K)$ and every continuous $f$ is a uniform limit of rational functions.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of $K$ gives the Riesz representation of the dual of $C(K)$.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Area zero is a statement about Lebesgue measure of $K$.
concepts.c:rational-approximation: The theorem says that $C(K)$ is the uniform closure of rational functions.
concepts.c:rational-function: Rational functions with poles off $K$ are the approximants.

source.note: The classical duality proof by the Cauchy transform, as in the treatments of rational approximation in Gamelin, Uniform Algebras (1969); not the original 1931 argument.

statement: Let $X$ be a [coherent space](c:coherent-space) and $\mathcal{K}(X)$ its quasi-compact open sets. Let $X^\vee$ have the same points, with basis the closed sets whose complements lie in $\mathcal{K}(X)$. Then $X^\vee$ is coherent, $\mathcal{K}(X^\vee) = \{X \setminus U : U \in \mathcal{K}(X)\}$ and $(X^\vee)^\vee = X$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [coherent](c:coherent-space): quasi-compact and sober, and its quasi-compact open sets form a base closed under finite intersection.

conclusion: The space $X^\vee$ is coherent with quasi-compact opens $\{X \setminus U : U \in \mathcal{K}(X)\}$, and $(X^\vee)^\vee = X$.

proofs.name: Prime filters of the opposite lattice
proofs.slogan: Identify $X$ with the prime filters of its lattice of quasi-compact opens, so that the dual space belongs to the opposite lattice.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The empty space and one-point spaces are included.

roles.why: Coherence makes $\mathcal{K}(X)$ a bounded [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) that is a base, so Stone duality recovers $X$ from it.

steps.slogan: Collect the quasi-compact opens into a bounded distributive lattice $L$.
steps.detail: Because $X$ is coherent, $L = \mathcal{K}(X)$ contains $\emptyset$ and $X$ and is closed under finite unions and intersections. So $L$ is a bounded [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice), and it is a base of the topology of $X$.

steps.slogan: Identify $X$ with the prime filters of $L$ by Stone duality.
steps.detail: By [Stone duality](c:stone-duality) for bounded distributive lattices, $x \mapsto F_x = \{U \in L : x \in U\}$ is a homeomorphism from $X$ onto the space of prime filters of $L$ with basic opens $\{F : U \in F\}$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the opposite lattice $L^{op}$ and its prime filters.
steps.detail: A prime filter of $L^{op}$ is a prime ideal of $L$, which is the complement of a prime filter of $L$. So $x \mapsto \{U \in L : x \notin U\}$ is a bijection from $X$ onto the prime filters of $L^{op}$.

steps.slogan: Match the topology of $X^\vee$ with the Stone topology of $L^{op}$.
steps.detail: Under this bijection the basic set $\{I : U \in I\}$ of $\mathrm{Spec}(L^{op})$ corresponds to $\{x : x \notin U\} = X \setminus U$. These sets are closed under finite intersection, since $(X \setminus U) \cap (X \setminus V) = X \setminus (U \cup V)$, and they are exactly the basic opens of $X^\vee$. So $X^\vee \cong \mathrm{Spec}(L^{op})$.

steps.slogan: Read off that $X^\vee$ is coherent with the stated quasi-compact opens.
steps.detail: By Stone duality, $\mathrm{Spec}(L^{op})$ is coherent and its quasi-compact opens are exactly the basic sets. Hence $X^\vee$ is coherent and $\mathcal{K}(X^\vee) = \{X \setminus U : U \in L\}$.

steps.slogan: Dualize again to recover the original topology.
steps.detail: The basic opens of $(X^\vee)^\vee$ are the closed sets of $X^\vee$ whose complement lies in $\mathcal{K}(X^\vee)$. Such a set $C$ has $X \setminus C = X \setminus U$ with $U \in L$, so $C = U$. Since $L$ is a base of $X$, the two topologies agree and $(X^\vee)^\vee = X$.

concepts.c:coherent-space: Coherent spaces are exactly the spaces that Stone duality describes by lattices.
concepts.c:distributive-lattice: The lattice of quasi-compact opens is distributive, so Stone duality applies.
concepts.c:stone-duality: Stone duality turns the topological dual into the opposite lattice.

source.note: Hochster, Prime ideal structure in commutative rings, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 142 (1969), introduces the dual; the proof here reduces it to Stone's duality for distributive lattices (1937).

statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [cartesian category](c:cartesian-category) and $\mathcal{D}$, $\mathcal{E}$ locally small $\mathcal{C}$-[indexed categories](c:indexed-category) with all indexed colimits, where $\mathcal{D}$ is well-copowered with a separating family. An indexed functor $F\colon \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}$ has an indexed right adjoint if and only if it is cocontinuous.

hypotheses.text: The base $\mathcal{C}$ is a [cartesian category](c:cartesian-category).
The categories $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{E}$ are locally small $\mathcal{C}$-[indexed categories](c:indexed-category) with all indexed colimits.
The indexed category $\mathcal{D}$ is well-copowered and has a separating family.
The map $F\colon \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{E}$ is an indexed functor.

conclusion: The functor $F$ has an indexed right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) if and only if $F$ preserves indexed colimits.

proofs.name: Fibrewise special adjoint functor theorem
proofs.slogan: Build the right adjoint fibre by fibre with the special adjoint functor theorem and check that the fibres fit together under reindexing.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The proof is an outline of Pare and Schumacher's argument; the full indexed details are in the cited work.

roles.why: Finite products in $\mathcal{C}$ give projections along which indexed coproducts and reindexing are compared.
Locally small indexed categories with indexed colimits make cocontinuity and the fibre functors meaningful.
Well-copowered with a separating family are the smallness conditions of the special adjoint functor theorem.
An indexed functor commutes with reindexing, which gives the mate comparison.

steps.slogan: Show that an indexed left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) preserves indexed colimits.
steps.detail: For an indexed adjunction $F \dashv G$, the hom-set bijections are natural in every fibre and compatible with reindexing. So maps out of $F(\mathrm{colim}\,D)$ correspond to compatible families of maps out of the $F(D_j)$, which says that $F$ preserves the indexed colimit.

steps.slogan: Reduce an indexed right adjoint to fibrewise right adjoints with a mate condition.
steps.detail: An indexed right adjoint of $F$ is a family of right adjoints $G_I$ of the fibre functors $F_I$ such that, for each map $u$ of $\mathcal{C}$, the mate $u^*G_I \Rightarrow G_J u^*$ of the isomorphism $F_J u^* \cong u^* F_I$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Obtain each fibrewise right adjoint from the special adjoint functor theorem.
steps.detail: The fibre functor $F_I$ is cocontinuous between cocomplete locally small categories, and the indexed smallness hypotheses on $\mathcal{D}$ are the indexed form of the smallness conditions of Freyd's special adjoint functor theorem. Pare and Schumacher prove that theorem in the indexed setting. It gives a right adjoint $G_I$ of every $F_I$.

steps.slogan: Show that indexed cocontinuity makes the mate comparison invertible.
steps.detail: Taking left adjoints, the mate condition for $G$ is equivalent to the statement that $F$ commutes with the indexed coproducts along the projections of $\mathcal{C}$. This holds because $F$ preserves indexed colimits. So the $G_I$ form an indexed functor.

steps.slogan: Assemble the fibrewise adjunctions into an indexed adjunction.
steps.detail: The units and counits of the adjunctions $F_I \dashv G_I$ are natural and compatible with reindexing by step 4. So they form an indexed adjunction $F \dashv G$, which proves sufficiency; step 1 proves necessity.

concepts.c:cartesian-category: Finite products in the base give the projections that reindexing uses.
concepts.c:indexed-category: The theorem is stated for locally small indexed categories.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The theorem characterizes when a functor is a left adjoint.

source.ref: R. Pare and D. Schumacher, Abstract families and the adjoint functor theorems, in: Indexed Categories and Their Applications, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 661, Springer, 1978, 1-125; see also P. T. Johnstone, Sketches of an Elephant, Volume 1, Oxford University Press, 2002, section B2.4
source.note: The outline follows the standard fibrewise route: the special adjoint functor theorem in each fibre and the Beck-Chevalley condition for reindexing.

statement: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be [monads](c:monad) on one category, with [distributive laws](c:distributive-law) $\lambda\colon BA \Rightarrow AB$, $\rho\colon CB \Rightarrow BC$ and $\sigma\colon CA \Rightarrow AC$ that satisfy the Yang-Baxter equation. Then $ABC$ is a monad with unit $\eta^A\eta^B\eta^C$, and its multiplication moves each factor past the others by the three laws.

hypotheses.text: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are [monads](c:monad) on one category $\mathcal{X}$.
The natural transformations $\lambda\colon BA \Rightarrow AB$, $\rho\colon CB \Rightarrow BC$ and $\sigma\colon CA \Rightarrow AC$ are [distributive laws](c:distributive-law).
The Yang-Baxter equation holds: $\lambda C \circ B\sigma \circ \rho A = A\rho \circ \sigma B \circ C\lambda$ as maps $CBA \Rightarrow ABC$.

conclusion: The composite functor $ABC$ is a monad with unit $\eta^A\eta^B\eta^C$ whose multiplication moves each factor past the others by the three laws.

proofs.name: Two applications of Beck's theorem
proofs.slogan: Compose $A$ and $B$ first, then compose $AB$ with $C$ by a derived distributive law that exists by the Yang-Baxter equation.
proofs.scope: The case of three monads. The same argument adds one monad at a time, which gives $n$ monads with laws that satisfy the Yang-Baxter equation for every triple.

roles.why: The units and multiplications of $A$, $B$ and $C$ give the monad structure of the composite.
The law $\lambda$ makes $AB$ a monad, and $\rho$ and $\sigma$ define the law of $C$ over $AB$.
The Yang-Baxter equation makes the new law compatible with the multiplication of $AB$.

steps.slogan: Form the monad $AB$ from the [distributive law](c:distributive-law) $\lambda$.
steps.detail: By Beck's theorem on distributive laws, $AB$ is a monad with unit $\eta^A\eta^B$ and multiplication $\mu^{AB} = \mu^A\mu^B \circ A\lambda B$.

steps.slogan: Define a candidate law $\tau\colon C(AB) \Rightarrow (AB)C$ from $\sigma$ and $\rho$.
steps.detail: Set $\tau = A\rho \circ \sigma B$, that is $CAB \Rightarrow ACB \Rightarrow ABC$. It moves $C$ past $A$ by $\sigma$ and then past $B$ by $\rho$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\tau$ respects the units and the multiplication of $C$.
steps.detail: Compatibility with the unit of $AB$, with $\eta^C$ and with $\mu^C$ follows factor by factor from the unit and multiplication axioms of $\sigma$ and $\rho$, and from naturality.

steps.slogan: Check with the Yang-Baxter equation that $\tau$ respects the multiplication of $AB$.
steps.detail: The multiplication $\mu^{AB} = \mu^A\mu^B \circ A\lambda B$ has $\lambda$ in the middle. Moving $C$ past it means passing $C$ across the pair $BA$ in two ways, once before and once after $\lambda$ acts. The two ways agree by the Yang-Baxter equation, and the other squares commute by the multiplication axioms of $\sigma$ and $\rho$.

steps.slogan: Apply Beck's theorem to $\tau$ to obtain the monad $ABC$.
steps.detail: Now $\tau$ is a [distributive law](c:distributive-law) of the monad $C$ over the monad $AB$. So $(AB)C$ is a monad with unit $\eta^{AB}\eta^C = \eta^A\eta^B\eta^C$ and multiplication $\mu^{AB}\mu^C \circ AB\tau C$, which expands into the three laws.

concepts.c:monad: The composite carries the structure of a monad.
concepts.c:distributive-law: Distributive laws are what compose two monads into one.

source.note: Direct proof by two uses of Beck's theorem on distributive laws; E. Cheng, Iterated distributive laws, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 150 (2011), 459-487, treats n monads and the 2-categorical meaning.

statement: Let $G \le S_n$ be a [primitive](c:primitive-group) [permutation group](c:permutation-group) that contains a cycle of prime length $p$ with $p \le n - 3$. Then $G$ contains the [alternating group](c:alternating-group) $A_n$, so $G = A_n$ or $G = S_n$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G \le S_n$ is a [primitive](c:primitive-group) permutation group on $n$ points.
The group $G$ contains a cycle of prime length $p$.
The cycle fixes at least three points, that is $p \le n - 3$.

proofs.name: Multiple transitivity and the classification
proofs.slogan: Prime length makes $G$ highly transitive, a pointwise stabilizer reduces to degree $p + 3$, and the classification of $4$-transitive groups finishes.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The last reduction step uses the classification of $4$-transitive groups, which depends on the classification of finite simple groups; Wielandt's elementary argument for that step is not reproduced.

roles.why: Primitivity is needed for Jordan's criterion and for the final step from a $3$-cycle to $A_n$.
A cycle of prime length is transitive of prime degree on its support, hence primitive there.
At least three fixed points give $4$-fold transitivity and room to restrict to degree $p + 3$.

steps.slogan: Show that the pointwise stabilizer of the fixed points is primitive on the support.
steps.detail: Let $c$ be the $p$-cycle, $\Delta$ its support and $\Gamma$ its set of fixed points. The pointwise stabilizer $G_{(\Gamma)}$ contains $\langle c \rangle$, which is transitive on the $p$ points of $\Delta$. A transitive group of prime degree is primitive, because block sizes divide $p$.

steps.slogan: Derive $(n - p + 1)$-fold transitivity of $G$ from Jordan's criterion.
steps.detail: Jordan's criterion (Wielandt, Finite Permutation Groups, 13.2) says that a primitive group, whose pointwise stabilizer of a set $\Gamma$ is primitive on the other points, is $(|\Gamma| + 1)$-fold transitive. Here $|\Gamma| = n - p \ge 3$, so $G$ is at least $4$-fold transitive.

steps.slogan: Restrict to degree $p + 3$ by fixing $n - p - 3$ fixed points of the cycle.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be a set of $n - p - 3$ fixed points of $c$. The pointwise stabilizer $G_{(T)}$ acts on the other $p + 3$ points. Because $G$ is $(n - p + 1)$-fold transitive, $G_{(T)}$ is $4$-fold transitive there, and it contains $c$.

steps.slogan: Identify the $4$-transitive group of degree $p + 3$ by the classification.
steps.detail: By the classification of finite simple groups, a $4$-transitive group of degree $m$ contains $A_m$ or is one of $M_{11}$, $M_{12}$, $M_{23}$, $M_{24}$, of degrees $11$, $12$, $23$, $24$. For these degrees $m - 3 \in \{8, 9, 20, 21\}$ is not prime, so $G_{(T)}$ contains $A_{p+3}$.

steps.slogan: Find a [3-cycle](c:3-cycle) in $G$ and conclude with Jordan's theorem on $3$-cycles.
steps.detail: Since $G_{(T)} \ge A_{p+3}$ and $p + 3 \ge 5$, the group $G$ contains a $3$-cycle. A primitive group that contains a $3$-cycle contains $A_n$ (Jordan 1871; Wielandt 13.3). So $A_n \le G$.

concepts.c:primitive-group: Primitivity drives both Jordan's criterion and the final step.
concepts.c:permutation-group: The group acts on $n$ points and is studied through its stabilizers.
concepts.c:alternating-group: The goal is to show that $G$ contains the alternating group.
concepts.c:3-cycle: A $3$-cycle in a primitive group forces the alternating group.

source.note: Steps 1 to 3 and 5 follow Wielandt, Finite Permutation Groups (1964), 13.2, 13.3 and 13.9, and Dixon and Mortimer, Permutation Groups, 3.3E. Step 4 replaces their elementary treatment of degree p + 3 by the classification of 4-transitive groups (Cameron 1981).

statement: Let $q$ be continuous on $[a, \infty)$ with $a > 0$, and consider the [differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $y'' + q(x)y = 0$. If $\liminf_{x\to\infty} x^2 q(x) > 1/4$, every nontrivial solution has infinitely many zeros. If $\limsup_{x\to\infty} x^2 q(x) < 1/4$, every nontrivial solution has finitely many zeros.

hypotheses.text: The coefficient $q$ is real and continuous on $[a, \infty)$ for some $a > 0$.
For the first claim: $\liminf_{x\to\infty} x^2 q(x) > 1/4$.
For the second claim: $\limsup_{x\to\infty} x^2 q(x) < 1/4$.

conclusion: In the first case every nontrivial solution oscillates, and in the second case no nontrivial solution does.

proofs.name: Sturm comparison with the Euler equation
proofs.slogan: Compare $y'' + qy = 0$ with the Euler equation $z'' + (c/x^2)z = 0$ by the Wronskian, using $c$ above or below $1/4$.
proofs.scope: This is Adolf Kneser's oscillation criterion. The other Kneser theorem, by Hellmuth Kneser, is about the topology of the solution set of an initial value problem and is not proved here.

roles.why: Continuity gives $C^2$ solutions whose zeros are simple, as the Wronskian argument needs.
It gives $q \ge c/x^2$ with $c > 1/4$ from some point on.
It gives $q \le c/x^2$ with $c < 1/4$ from some point on.

steps.slogan: Compare $q$ with $c/x^2$ for a constant $c$ near the threshold $1/4$.
steps.detail: In the first case pick $c$ with $1/4 < c < \liminf x^2 q$, so $q(x) \ge c/x^2$ for $x \ge x_0$. In the second case pick $c$ with $\limsup x^2 q < c < 1/4$, so $q(x) \le c/x^2$ for $x \ge x_0$.

steps.slogan: Solve the Euler equation $z'' + (c/x^2)z = 0$ explicitly.
steps.detail: The function $x^r$ solves it when $r^2 - r + c = 0$. For $c > 1/4$, $z = \sqrt{x}\cos(\omega\ln x)$ with $\omega = \sqrt{c - 1/4}$ solves it and has zeros $t_k = \exp((\pi/2 + k\pi)/\omega) \to \infty$. For $c < 1/4$, $z = x^r$ with $r = (1 + \sqrt{1 - 4c})/2$ is positive on $(0, \infty)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the derivative of the [Wronskian](c:wronskian) of $y$ and $z$.
steps.detail: Let $q_0 = c/x^2$, $y'' + qy = 0$ and $z'' + q_0 z = 0$. The Wronskian $W = yz' - y'z$ has $W' = yz'' - y''z = (q - q_0)\,yz$. This identity is the proof of the Sturm-Picone comparison theorem.

steps.slogan: In the first case show that $y$ has a zero between consecutive zeros of $z$.
steps.detail: Let $t_k < t_{k+1}$ be consecutive zeros of $z$ with $t_k \ge x_0$, and suppose $y > 0$ on $[t_k, t_{k+1}]$. Then $W(t_k) = y(t_k)z'(t_k) > 0 > W(t_{k+1})$, but $W' = (q - q_0)yz \ge 0$ forces $W(t_{k+1}) \ge W(t_k)$. So $y$ has a zero in every interval $[t_{2k}, t_{2k+1}]$, and these intervals are disjoint.

steps.slogan: In the second case show that $y$ cannot have two zeros beyond $x_0$.
steps.detail: Suppose $y$ has consecutive zeros $x_1 < x_2$ in $[x_0, \infty)$ with $y > 0$ between them. Then $y'(x_1) > 0 > y'(x_2)$, so $W(x_1) = -y'(x_1)z(x_1) < 0 < W(x_2)$ because $z > 0$, but $W' = (q - q_0)yz \le 0$ forces $W(x_2) \le W(x_1)$. So $y$ has at most one zero in $[x_0, \infty)$ and finitely many in $[a, \infty)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases into the oscillation criterion.
steps.detail: The first case gives infinitely many zeros for every nontrivial solution, and the second case gives finitely many. These are the two claims of the criterion.

concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: The criterion concerns zeros of solutions of a second-order equation.
concepts.c:wronskian: The Wronskian of $y$ and $z$ has a derivative with a sign, which gives the comparison.

source.note: Classical Sturm comparison with the Euler equation, as in Kneser's 1893 oscillation criterion (A. Kneser, Math. Ann. 42, 1893).

statement: Let $X$ be a [reflexive](c:reflexive-space) [Banach space](c:banach-space) and $f\colon [0, T] \to X$ an [absolutely continuous function](c:absolutely-continuous-function). Then $f$ is differentiable almost everywhere, $f'$ is Bochner integrable, and $f(t) = f(0) + \int_0^t f'(s)\,ds$ for all $t$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [reflexive](c:reflexive-space) [Banach space](c:banach-space).
The function $f\colon [0, T] \to X$ is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-function).

conclusion: The function $f$ is differentiable at almost every $t$, and $f$ is the indefinite Bochner integral of $f'$.

proofs.name: Lipschitz case and arc length
proofs.slogan: Prove the Lipschitz case by a weak-star limit of difference quotients, then reparametrize an absolutely continuous function by arc length.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. For $X = \mathbb{R}$ it is Lebesgue's differentiation theorem for absolutely continuous functions.

roles.why: Reflexivity makes bounded sets in $L^\infty(0, S; X)$ weak-star sequentially compact.
Absolute continuity gives an absolutely continuous variation function, so arc length makes $f$ Lipschitz.

steps.slogan: Reparametrize $f$ by its variation function so that it becomes Lipschitz.
steps.detail: Let $v(t)$ be the total variation of $f$ on $[0, t]$. For absolutely continuous $f$, $v$ is nondecreasing and absolutely continuous. Since $\|f(t) - f(t')\| \le v(t') - v(t)$, the map $h(v(t)) = f(t)$ is well defined on $[0, v(T)]$ and is $1$-Lipschitz.

steps.slogan: Take a weak-star limit of the difference quotients of the Lipschitz map $h$.
steps.detail: Replace $X$ by the closed span $X_0$ of $h([0, S])$, which is separable and reflexive, so $X_0^*$ is separable. The quotients $g_n(s) = n(h(s + 1/n) - h(s))$ have norm at most $1$ in $L^\infty(0, S; X_0) = L^1(0, S; X_0^*)^*$. By the sequential Banach-Alaoglu theorem a subsequence converges weak-star to some $g$.

steps.slogan: Show that $h$ is the integral of the weak-star limit $g$.
steps.detail: For $\xi \in X_0^*$, $\int_0^t g_n\,ds = n\int_t^{t+1/n} h - n\int_0^{1/n} h \to h(t) - h(0)$ by continuity. Weak-star convergence turns the left side into $\int_0^t \langle \xi, g \rangle\,ds$. So $h(t) = h(0) + \int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ as a Bochner integral.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the Bochner integral at its Lebesgue points.
steps.detail: The function $g$ is Bochner integrable, so almost every $t$ is a Lebesgue point: $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\int_t^{t+\varepsilon} \|g(s) - g(t)\|\,ds \to 0$. At such a point $h'(t) = g(t)$ in norm. So $h$ is differentiable almost everywhere with $h' = g$.

steps.slogan: Transfer differentiability and the integral formula from $h$ back to $f$.
steps.detail: By steps 3 and 4, $f(t) = h(v(t)) = f(0) + \int_0^{v(t)} h'(s)\,ds$. The change of variables $s = v(\tau)$ for the absolutely continuous nondecreasing $v$ gives $f(t) = f(0) + \int_0^t h'(v(\tau))\,v'(\tau)\,d\tau$. So $f$ is an indefinite Bochner integral, and Lebesgue differentiation gives $f' = h'(v)\,v'$ almost everywhere.

concepts.c:reflexive-space: Reflexivity gives weak-star compactness of the difference quotients.
concepts.c:banach-space: The target is a Banach space, where Bochner integrals are defined.
concepts.c:absolutely-continuous-function: Absolute continuity gives the Lipschitz reparametrization and the integral formula.

source.note: The standard route through Lipschitz maps and the Radon-Nikodym property of reflexive spaces, after Komura (1967) and as presented in Arendt, Batty, Hieber and Neubrander, Vector-valued Laplace Transforms and Cauchy Problems.

statement: Let $\{v_k\}$ be a [closed](c:completeness) [orthonormal set](c:orthonormal-set) in a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$, for example $L^2(a, b)$, and let $\{u_k\}$ be an orthonormal set in $H$. Then $\{u_k\}$ is closed if and only if, for every $k$, the series $\sum_j \langle v_k, u_j \rangle u_j$ converges in mean to $v_k$.

hypotheses.text: The orthonormal set $\{v_k\}$ is closed: only the zero vector is orthogonal to every $v_k$.
The family $\{u_k\}$ is an orthonormal set in $H$.

conclusion: The set $\{u_k\}$ is closed exactly when each $v_k$ is the mean-limit of its $u$-series.

proofs.name: Orthogonal complement
proofs.slogan: A vector orthogonal to all $u_j$ is orthogonal to all $v_k$ by mean convergence, and closedness means that no nonzero vector is orthogonal.
proofs.scope: Both directions of the equivalence, in a real or complex Hilbert space. Closed means maximal; step 1 shows that this is equivalent to mean convergence of Fourier series and to Parseval's identity.

roles.why: Closedness of $\{v_k\}$ turns a vector orthogonal to all $v_k$ into zero.
Orthonormality of $\{u_k\}$ gives Bessel's inequality and the meaning of the $u$-series.

steps.slogan: Restate closedness of an orthonormal set as mean convergence of Fourier series.
steps.detail: For an orthonormal set $\{w_k\}$ in $H$ these are equivalent: only $0$ is orthogonal to all $w_k$, every $f$ is the mean-limit of $\sum \langle f, w_k \rangle w_k$, and Parseval's identity holds for every $f$. Bessel's inequality gives convergence of the series, and its sum differs from $f$ by a vector orthogonal to every $w_k$.

steps.slogan: Expand each $v_k$ in the $u$-series when $\{u_k\}$ is closed.
steps.detail: If $\{u_k\}$ is closed, step 1 gives that every vector, and in particular each $v_k$, is the mean-limit of its $u$-series. This is the necessity of the condition.

steps.slogan: Pair a vector orthogonal to all $u_j$ with the mean-convergent series of $v_k$.
steps.detail: Assume each $v_k$ is the mean-limit of the partial sums $S_N = \sum_{j \le N} \langle v_k, u_j \rangle u_j$, and let $f \perp u_j$ for all $j$. Then $\langle f, S_N \rangle = 0$ for every $N$. Continuity of the inner product gives $\langle f, v_k \rangle = \lim_N \langle f, S_N \rangle = 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $f = 0$ because $\{v_k\}$ is closed.
steps.detail: By step 3, $f$ is orthogonal to every $v_k$, and $\{v_k\}$ is closed, so $f = 0$. Hence only $0$ is orthogonal to all $u_j$, which is closedness of $\{u_k\}$ by step 1.

steps.slogan: Combine the two implications into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 2 shows that closedness of $\{u_k\}$ implies mean convergence for every $v_k$, and steps 3 and 4 show the converse. So the two conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:orthonormal-set: The proof uses orthogonality of vectors to the members of the sets.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Inner products, orthogonality and mean convergence live in the Hilbert space.
concepts.c:completeness: Closedness of an orthonormal set is its completeness: no nonzero orthogonal vector.

source.note: The standard Hilbert-space argument for the criterion that G. Lauricella proved in 1912 for orthogonal functions.

statement: Let $R$ be a ring with identity that is right [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring). Then every [nil](c:nil-ideal) one-sided ideal of $R$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-ideal).

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ has an identity element.
The ring $R$ is right [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring): its right ideals satisfy the ascending chain condition.
The set $A$ is a one-sided ideal of $R$ in which every element is nilpotent, so $A$ is [nil](c:nil-ideal).

conclusion: Some power $A^m$ is zero, so $A$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-ideal).

proofs.name: Maximal annihilator
proofs.slogan: Divide by the largest nilpotent ideal, then show by a maximal annihilator that a nil right ideal of the quotient is zero.
proofs.scope: Nil left ideals and nil right ideals. Left ideals reduce to right ideals by passing to $AR$.

roles.why: The identity puts $a$ into $RaR$ and makes $AR$ nonzero when $A$ is nonzero.
The ascending chain condition gives a largest nilpotent ideal and a maximal right annihilator.
Nilpotency of every element of the ideal gives $(ax)^n = 0$ for $ax$ in the ideal.

steps.slogan: Find the largest nilpotent two-sided ideal $N$ of $R$.
steps.detail: By the ascending chain condition there is a maximal nilpotent two-sided ideal $N$. If $I^m = 0$ and $J^n = 0$, then $(I + J)^m \subseteq J$ and $(I + J)^{mn} = 0$, so $N + J$ is nilpotent for every nilpotent ideal $J$. Hence $N$ contains every nilpotent ideal.

steps.slogan: Pass to $\bar R = R/N$, which has no nonzero nilpotent ideal.
steps.detail: If $J/N$ is nilpotent in $R/N$, then $J^k \subseteq N$ and $N^m = 0$ give $J^{km} = 0$, so $J \subseteq N$. The ring $\bar R$ is right Noetherian, and the image of a nil one-sided ideal $A$ is nil. It remains to show that $\bar R$ has no nonzero nil one-sided ideal, because then $A \subseteq N$ and $A^m \subseteq N^m = 0$.

steps.slogan: Reduce a nil left ideal to a nil right ideal.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be a nil left ideal of $\bar R$. Then $B\bar R$ is a right ideal, and it is nil because $(br)^{n+1} = b(rb)^n r$ with $rb \in B$ nilpotent. It is nonzero when $B \ne 0$, since $1 \in \bar R$. So it suffices to treat nil right ideals.

steps.slogan: Choose $a \ne 0$ in a nil right ideal $B$ with maximal right [annihilator](c:annihilator).
steps.detail:
Suppose $B 
e 0$ is a nil right ideal of $ ar R$. The right annihilators $r(b) = \{x : bx = 0\}$ with $0 
e b \in B$ are right ideals, so the ascending chain condition gives some $a 
e 0$ in $B$ with $r(a)$ maximal among them.

steps.slogan: Show that $a\bar R a = 0$ by following the powers of $ax$.
steps.detail:
Suppose $axa 
e 0$. Each $(ax)^k a$ lies in $B$ and has $r((ax)^k a) \supseteq r(a)$, so $(ax)^k a 
e 0$ gives $r((ax)^k a) = r(a)$ by maximality. If $(ax)^{k+1}a = 0$, then $xa \in r((ax)^k a) = r(a)$, so $axa = 0$, which is false. So $(ax)^k a 
e 0$ for all $k$, against $(ax)^n = 0$ for the nilpotent $ax \in B$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\bar R a \bar R$ is a nonzero nilpotent ideal, which is impossible.
steps.detail: From $a\bar R a = 0$ we get $(\bar R a \bar R)^2 = \bar R a \bar R a \bar R = 0$, and $a \in \bar R a \bar R$ is nonzero. This is a nonzero nilpotent ideal of $\bar R$, which does not exist. So $\bar R$ has no nonzero nil one-sided ideal, and $A \subseteq N$ is nilpotent.

concepts.c:noetherian-ring: The chain condition gives the largest nilpotent ideal and the maximal annihilator.
concepts.c:nil-ideal: Every element of the ideal is nilpotent, which the power argument uses.
concepts.c:nilpotent-ideal: The ideal must have a vanishing power, not only nilpotent elements.
concepts.c:annihilator: A maximal right annihilator controls which products of $a$ vanish.

source.note: The classical proof of Levitzki (1945) in the form with maximal annihilators found in standard texts, for example Lam, A First Course in Noncommutative Rings.

statement: In dimension $4$, let $A^{ij}$ be a symmetric tensor that depends on a pseudo-Riemannian metric $g$ and its first and second derivatives, and has $\nabla_i A^{ij} = 0$ for every metric. Then $A^{ij} = a\,G^{ij} + b\,g^{ij}$ for constants $a$ and $b$, where $G^{ij}$ is the [Einstein tensor](c:einstein-tensor).

hypotheses.text: The spacetime has dimension $4$.
The tensor $A^{ij}$ is symmetric and is a natural function of $g_{ij}$, $\partial g$ and $\partial^2 g$.
The divergence vanishes: $\nabla_i A^{ij} = 0$ for every metric.

conclusion: The tensor is $A^{ij} = aG^{ij} + bg^{ij}$, so $A^{ij} = 0$ is the [Einstein field equations](c:einstein-field-equations) with a cosmological constant.

proofs.name: Reduction to curvature and index count
proofs.slogan: Reduce $A$ to a curvature expression, solve the divergence condition, and count indices in dimension $4$.
proofs.scope: Dimension $4$, as stated. The action form follows because the Euler-Lagrange tensor of a diffeomorphism-invariant [Lagrangian](c:lagrangian) is symmetric and divergence-free, so a Lagrangian with second-order field equations gives Einstein's equations with a cosmological constant.

roles.why: Dimension $4$ removes the Lovelock terms of order $2$ and higher, which need at least $5$ indices.
Naturality allows $A$ to be computed in normal coordinates, where it depends on $g$ and the curvature only.
The divergence condition is linear in third derivatives of $g$ and restricts the dependence on the curvature.

steps.slogan: Show that $A^{ij}$ depends on the metric and its curvature only.
steps.detail: At a point, choose normal coordinates in which $\partial g = 0$. Naturality of $A$ then reduces it to a function of $g$ and the Riemann tensor $R_{ijkl}$ alone.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the divergence condition to get an algebraic condition on $\partial A/\partial R$.
steps.detail:
The condition $
abla_i A^{ij} = 0$ contains third derivatives of $g$ only through $
abla R$, and linearly. The value of $
abla R$ at a point is free apart from the Bianchi identity, so the coefficients $\partial A^{ij}/\partial R_{klmn}$ satisfy an algebraic identity modulo Bianchi.

steps.slogan: Solve the algebraic condition to write $A$ with the generalized Kronecker delta.
steps.detail: The cited work shows that the condition forces $A^i{}_j = \sum_k c_k\,\delta^{i i_1 \dots i_{2k}}_{j j_1 \dots j_{2k}} R^{j_1 j_2}{}_{i_1 i_2} \cdots R^{j_{2k-1} j_{2k}}{}_{i_{2k-1} i_{2k}}$ with constants $c_k$.

steps.slogan: Count indices to remove every term with $k \ge 2$ in dimension $4$.
steps.detail: The generalized Kronecker delta with $2k + 1$ upper indices vanishes when $2k + 1 > 4$. So only $k = 0$, which is the metric, and $k = 1$, which is the Einstein tensor, remain.

steps.slogan: Read off $A^{ij} = aG^{ij} + bg^{ij}$ from the two remaining terms.
steps.detail: The term with $k = 0$ is $c_0 g^{ij}$, and the term with $k = 1$ is proportional to the [Einstein tensor](c:einstein-tensor) $G^{ij}$. So $A^{ij} = aG^{ij} + bg^{ij}$, and $A^{ij} = 0$ is the [Einstein field equations](c:einstein-field-equations) with a cosmological constant.

concepts.c:einstein-tensor: The surviving $k = 1$ term is the Einstein tensor.
concepts.c:einstein-field-equations: Setting $A^{ij} = 0$ gives Einstein's equations with a cosmological constant.
concepts.c:lagrangian: A Lagrangian's Euler-Lagrange tensor supplies the symmetric divergence-free tensor.

source.ref: D. Lovelock, The Einstein tensor and its generalizations, Journal of Mathematical Physics 12 (1971), 498-502
source.note: The steps outline Lovelock's argument: reduction to the curvature, the divergence identity, the Lovelock tensors, and the index count in dimension 4.

statement: For every [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $X$ and every commutative $\sigma$-complete [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$, the $\sigma$-homomorphisms $A \to B(X)$ correspond bijectively and naturally to the measurable maps $X \to \mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A$. Here $B(X)$ is the algebra of bounded measurable functions and $\mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A$ the space of $\sigma$-characters of $A$.

hypotheses.text: The set $X$ is a [measurable space](c:measurable-space).
The algebra $A$ is a commutative unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) in which every bounded increasing sequence of self-adjoint elements has a supremum.

conclusion: There is a bijection $\mathrm{Hom}_\sigma(A, B(X)) \cong \mathrm{Meas}(X, \mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A)$, natural in $A$ and $X$, so $B$ and $\mathrm{Spec}_\sigma$ form a contravariant [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor).

proofs.name: Hom-set bijection by evaluation
proofs.slogan: Match a $\sigma$-homomorphism into $B(X)$ with the family of its pointwise evaluations, which is a measurable map into the space of $\sigma$-characters.
proofs.scope: All commutative $\sigma$-C*-algebras $A$ and all measurable spaces $X$. A $\sigma$-homomorphism is a unital $*$-homomorphism that preserves suprema of bounded increasing sequences, and $\mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A$ carries the [$\sigma$-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) generated by the maps $\chi \mapsto \chi(a)$.

roles.why: The measurable structure of $X$ defines $B(X)$ and makes measurability of the induced map meaningful.
The $\sigma$-completeness of $A$ defines $\sigma$-characters and the space $\mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A$.

steps.slogan: Show that evaluation at a point is a $\sigma$-character of $B(X)$.
steps.detail: A bounded increasing sequence in $B(X)$ has a pointwise supremum that is bounded and measurable, and this is its supremum in $B(X)$. So $\mathrm{ev}_x\colon B(X) \to \mathbb{C}$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism that preserves such suprema.

steps.slogan: Define $\mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A$ with the smallest $\sigma$-algebra that makes the evaluations measurable.
steps.detail: Let $\mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A$ be the set of $\sigma$-characters $\chi\colon A \to \mathbb{C}$. Give it the smallest [$\sigma$-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) for which every $\hat a\colon \chi \mapsto \chi(a)$ is measurable.

steps.slogan: Send a $\sigma$-homomorphism $\varphi\colon A \to B(X)$ to the map $x \mapsto \mathrm{ev}_x \circ \varphi$.
steps.detail: By step 1, each $\mathrm{ev}_x \circ \varphi$ is a composite of $\sigma$-homomorphisms, so it is a $\sigma$-character. The map $g_\varphi(x) = \mathrm{ev}_x \circ \varphi$ is measurable because $\hat a \circ g_\varphi = \varphi(a)$ is measurable for every $a$.

steps.slogan: Send a measurable map $g\colon X \to \mathrm{Spec}_\sigma A$ to the map $a \mapsto \hat a \circ g$.
steps.detail: The function $\hat a \circ g$ is measurable, and bounded by $\|a\|$ because characters are contractive. The assignment is a unital $*$-homomorphism because each $g(x)$ is one. It preserves suprema of bounded increasing sequences, because suprema in $B(X)$ are pointwise and each $g(x)$ preserves them.

steps.slogan: Check that the two assignments are inverse to each other and natural.
steps.detail: Starting from $\varphi$, steps 3 and 4 return $a \mapsto (x \mapsto \varphi(a)(x)) = \varphi(a)$. Starting from $g$, they return $x \mapsto (a \mapsto g(x)(a)) = g(x)$. Naturality in $A$ is precomposition with $\sigma$-homomorphisms and in $X$ is precomposition with measurable maps, and both assignments respect these.

concepts.c:measurable-space: Measurability of maps out of $X$ is what the bijection counts.
concepts.c:c-star-algebra: The algebras are commutative C*-algebras, and characters are contractive.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The bijection of hom-sets is the statement that the two functors are adjoint.
concepts.c:sigma-algebra: The measurable structure on the space of characters is a $\sigma$-algebra.

source.note: Direct proof of the hom-set bijection; the nLab entry on measurable Gelfand duality obtains the adjunction by composing the equivalence of sigma-C*-algebras with Boolean sigma-algebras and Loomis-Sikorski duality.

statement: Let $F_1 \dashv U_1\colon \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}_1$ be an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor) with [monad](c:monad) $T_1 = U_1F_1$, let $\mathcal{C}_2$ be the [Eilenberg-Moore category](c:eilenberg-moore-category) of $T_1$, and $U_2\colon \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}_2$ the [comparison functor](c:comparison-functor). If $\mathcal{D}$ has [reflexive coequalizers](c:has-reflexive-coequalizers), then $U_2$ has a left adjoint $F_2$, and the construction repeats.

hypotheses.text: The functors form an adjunction $F_1 \dashv U_1$ with $U_1\colon \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}_1$.
The category $\mathcal{D}$ has [reflexive coequalizers](c:has-reflexive-coequalizers).

conclusion: The comparison functor $U_2$ has a left adjoint $F_2$, and iterating gives adjunctions $F_n \dashv U_n\colon \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}_n$ for every $n$.

proofs.name: Left adjoint by reflexive coequalizers
proofs.slogan: Build $F_2$ on an algebra as a reflexive coequalizer in $\mathcal{D}$, check the hom-set bijection, and repeat.
proofs.scope: The existence of $F_2$ and the iteration. At stage $n + 1$ the hypotheses are the same, because $\mathcal{D}$ does not change.

roles.why: The adjunction supplies the unit, the counit, the monad $T_1$ and the transposition of maps.
Reflexive coequalizers in $\mathcal{D}$ give the object $F_2(A, a)$ and the next stage.

steps.slogan: Write the [comparison functor](c:comparison-functor) $U_2$ explicitly.
steps.detail: With counit $\varepsilon$, $U_2(d) = (U_1 d, U_1\varepsilon_d)$ and $U_2 g = U_1 g$. The pair $(U_1 d, U_1\varepsilon_d)$ is an algebra for $T_1$ by the triangle identities.

steps.slogan: Attach a [reflexive pair](c:is-reflexive-pair) in $\mathcal{D}$ to each $T_1$-algebra $(A, a)$.
steps.detail: The maps $F_1 a$ and $\varepsilon_{F_1A}$ both go from $F_1U_1F_1A$ to $F_1A$. They have the common section $F_1\eta_A$, because $a\eta_A = 1$ and the triangle identity gives $\varepsilon_{F_1A} \circ F_1\eta_A = 1$.

steps.slogan: Define $F_2(A, a)$ as the [coequalizer](c:coequalizer) of this reflexive pair.
steps.detail: Since $\mathcal{D}$ has [reflexive coequalizers](c:has-reflexive-coequalizers), the coequalizer $q\colon F_1A \to F_2(A, a)$ exists. A map $g\colon F_1A \to d$ factors through $q$ exactly when $g \circ F_1 a = g \circ \varepsilon_{F_1A}$.

steps.slogan: Show that maps out of $F_2(A, a)$ match algebra maps into $U_2 d$.
steps.detail: Let $g^\flat = U_1 g \circ \eta_A$ be the transpose of $g\colon F_1A \to d$. The condition $g \circ F_1 a = g \circ \varepsilon_{F_1A}$ transposes to $U_1 g = g^\flat \circ a$. Since $U_1 g = U_1\varepsilon_d \circ T_1 g^\flat$, this says that $g^\flat$ is a $T_1$-algebra map $(A, a) \to U_2 d$. So $\mathcal{D}(F_2(A, a), d) \cong \mathcal{C}_2((A, a), U_2 d)$, naturally.

steps.slogan: Repeat the construction with the new adjunction $F_2 \dashv U_2$.
steps.detail: The adjunction $F_2 \dashv U_2$ has the same $\mathcal{D}$, so the hypothesis holds again. It gives the monad $T_2 = U_2F_2$ on $\mathcal{C}_2$, its Eilenberg-Moore category $\mathcal{C}_3$, and a comparison functor with a left adjoint. Induction gives every $n$.

concepts.c:adjoint-functor: Adjunctions give the transposition of maps and the monads of the tower.
concepts.c:monad: Each adjunction induces a monad whose algebras form the next category.
concepts.c:eilenberg-moore-category: The categories of algebras are the stages of the decomposition.
concepts.c:comparison-functor: The comparison functor is the right adjoint that the proof constructs a left adjoint for.
concepts.c:has-reflexive-coequalizers: Reflexive coequalizers in $\mathcal{D}$ build the left adjoint.
concepts.c:is-reflexive-pair: The pair of maps has a common section, which makes it reflexive.
concepts.c:coequalizer: The coequalizer is the value of the left adjoint on an algebra.

source.note: The left adjoint of the comparison functor under reflexive coequalizers is the classical construction used for Beck's monadicity theorem (Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, VI.7); the iteration is as in the nLab entry on monadic decomposition.

statement: Let $X$ be a simply connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex) with $A_n = H_n(X)$. Then $X$ is homotopy equivalent to a union of CW complexes $* = X_1 \subset X_2 \subset \cdots$, where $X_n$ is $X_{n-1}$ with the cone on a [Moore space](c:moore-space) $M(A_n, n-1)$ attached, $H_i(X_n) \cong A_i$ for $i \le n$ and $H_i(X_n) = 0$ for $i > n$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [CW complex](c:cw-complex).
The space $X$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).

conclusion: There are CW complexes $X_n$ and compatible maps $f_n\colon X_n \to X$ as described, and the induced map from $\bigcup X_n$ to $X$ is a homotopy equivalence.

proofs.name: Homotopy fibre and Whitehead's theorem
proofs.slogan: Build $X_n$ from $X_{n-1}$ by killing the homotopy fibre's first group, compare homology, and finish with Whitehead's theorem.
proofs.scope: Simply connected $X$ of any homology type. The first stage uses $M(A_2, 1)$, which is not simply connected.

roles.why: A CW structure lets the cone attachments be taken cellular, so each $X_n$ is a CW complex.
Simple connectivity of $X$ and of each $X_{n-1}$ gives the Hurewicz isomorphism and the final use of Whitehead's theorem.

steps.slogan: Compute the homotopy fibre $F$ of $f_{n-1}$ with the Hurewicz theorem.
steps.detail: Assume that $f_{n-1}\colon X_{n-1} \to X$ is a [homology](c:homology) isomorphism in degrees $\le n-1$ and that $H_i(X_{n-1}) = 0$ for $i \ge n$; start with $X_1 = *$. The cofibre $C$ of $f_{n-1}$ has $H_i(C) = 0$ for $i < n$ and $H_n(C) \cong A_n$. The relative Hurewicz theorem then makes $F$ $(n-2)$-connected with $\pi_{n-1}(F) \cong H_{n-1}(F) \cong A_n$.

steps.slogan: Attach the cone on a Moore space along a map $g_n$ to form $X_n$.
steps.detail: Choose a map $M(A_n, n-1) \to F$ that is an isomorphism on $H_{n-1}$; it exists because $F$ is $(n-2)$-connected and $\pi_{n-1}(F) \cong A_n$. Let $g_n$ be its composite with $F \to X_{n-1}$, and put $X_n = X_{n-1} \cup_{g_n} C\,M(A_n, n-1)$. The null-homotopy of $f_{n-1}g_n$ from the lift to $F$ extends $f_{n-1}$ to $f_n\colon X_n \to X$.

steps.slogan: Compute the homology of $X_n$ from the cofibration sequence.
steps.detail: The quotient $X_n/X_{n-1}$ is the [Moore space](c:moore-space) $\Sigma M(A_n, n-1) = M(A_n, n)$. The boundary map $H_n(X_n/X_{n-1}) \to H_{n-1}(X_{n-1})$ is zero, because $F \to X_{n-1} \to X$ is null-homotopic and $H_{n-1}(X_{n-1}) \to H_{n-1}(X)$ is injective. So $H_n(X_n) \cong A_n$, and $H_i(X_n) = H_i(X_{n-1})$ for $i < n$ and $0$ for $i > n$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f_n$ is a homology isomorphism in degrees up to $n$.
steps.detail: Compare the long exact sequences of $(X_n, X_{n-1})$ and of the cofibre $C$ of $f_{n-1}$. The map $M(A_n, n) \to C$ is an isomorphism on $H_n$ by naturality of the Hurewicz maps. The five lemma gives that $f_n$ is an isomorphism on $H_i$ for $i \le n$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the union and apply Whitehead's theorem.
steps.detail: Let $X_\infty = \bigcup X_n$ and $f_\infty = \bigcup f_n$. Each $X_n$ is simply connected by van Kampen, and $H_i(X_\infty) = H_i(X_n)$ for $n \ge i$, so $f_\infty$ is a homology isomorphism of simply connected CW complexes. By Whitehead's theorem it is a homotopy equivalence.

concepts.c:cw-complex: Cellular attachments keep every stage a CW complex.
concepts.c:moore-space: Moore spaces are the pieces whose cones are attached at each stage.
concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity allows the Hurewicz and Whitehead theorems.
concepts.c:homology: The stages are built to reproduce the homology of $X$ one degree at a time.

source.note: The homology decomposition of Eckmann and Hilton, built stage by stage as in the nLab entries on the Moore decomposition and Moore spaces, and finished with Whitehead's theorem.
